steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Hormones focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Hormones.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Adjunctive or alternative therapy for treatment escalation in Hormones.
drug_classes.dosing: Introduce second-line agent as add-on dual therapy or sequential switch; reassess at 4–6 weeks.
drug_classes.pearls: Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Hormones require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Targeted intervention for severe or refractory Hormones.
drug_classes.dosing: Specialist-guided dosing with pre-treatment laboratory clearance and structured monitoring.
drug_classes.pearls: Perform required baseline screening (e.g. latent infections, CBC, organ function panels) prior to initiation.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Hormones.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Adjust metformin dose when eGFR 30–44 mL/min/1.73m²; avoid if eGFR < 30.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Monitor liver function when using insulin sensitizers (TZDs) or GLP-1 receptor agonists.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Insulin is the preferred agent for glycemic management during pregnancy and lactation.
special_populations.elderly: Relax HbA1c targets (< 7.5–8.0%) in elderly to minimize risk of cognitive impairment from hypoglycemia.

style_3_monograph.summary: Hormones are your body's chemical messengers. They travel in your bloodstream to tissues or organs. They work slowly, over time, and affect many different processes, including: Growth and development Metabolism - how your body gets energy from the foods you eat Sexual function Reproduction Mood Endocrine glands, which are special groups of cells, make hormones. The major endocrine glands are the pituitary, pineal, thymus, thyroid, adrenal glands, and pancreas. In addition, men produce hormones in their testes and women produce them in their ovaries. Hormones are powerful. It takes only a tiny amount to cause big changes in cells or even your whole body. That is why too much or too little of a certain hormone can be serious. Laboratory tests can measure the hormone levels in your blood, urine, or saliva. Your health care provider may perform these tests if you have symptoms of a hormone disorder . Home pregnancy tests are similar - they test for pregnancy hormones in your urine.
style_3_monograph.treatment: Consult healthcare provider for individualized management.
